result.summary: Macareus tells how his crew landed at Circe's isle, where she turned them into swine with a drugged drink. Eurylochus escaped and warned Ulysses, who used the herb moly to overcome Circe and made her restore his men. After a year there, a handmaid begins to tell Macareus the story of a marble statue.

scenes.title: Editor's argument of the fable
scenes.summary: A prose headnote summarizes the episode of Circe's transformation of the crew.

scenes.title: Arrival at Circe's palace
scenes.summary: Chosen by lot, Macareus and his companions go to Circe's palace past tame beasts and are welcomed by her and her herb-sorting nymphs. She serves them a drugged mixture.
scenes.stakes: The men walk unknowingly into the enchantress's trap.

scenes.title: Transformed into swine
scenes.summary: Circe touches the men with her wand and they become swine and are shut in a sty. Only Eurylochus escapes.
scenes.stakes: The men lose human shape and speech.

scenes.title: Ulysses rescues his men
scenes.summary: Armed with moly from Mercury, Ulysses resists Circe, forces her to promise, and demands his men back. She restores them and they weep with gratitude.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks the same fate; his men risk remaining swine forever.

scenes.title: The statue in the temple
scenes.summary: During a year's stay, a handmaid shows Macareus a marble statue with a woodpecker and begins to explain it.

alias_notes.explanation: Mercury was born on Mount Cyllene and is a divine messenger.
The headnote uses Achæmenides, but the narrator is named Macareus in the text.

notable_quotes.reason: Names the magical herb moly, given by Mercury as protection against Circe.

analysis.text: Transformation as loss of identity: the men keep human minds but lose speech and form, and Macareus is ashamed to tell it.
Ovid retells Homer's Odyssey episode from a lesser crewman's view, with divine help and cunning defeating magic.

legacy.text: The Circe episode, from Homer and Ovid, inspired countless later artworks and poems depicting men turned into beasts.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's Macareus is a companion of Ulysses who appears in Homer's tale only indirectly, since Homer does not name him.

language_notes.text: The headnote names Achæmenides as narrator, but the speaker in the text is Macareus, who tells the tale. Both are Ulysses' former crewmen, and the translator's headnote confuses them.
Antiphates, king of the Laestrygonian cannibals, and the Cyclop Polyphemus had earlier destroyed or devoured Ulysses' men, so the crew fear another strange land.
"Twice nine" means eighteen; the party is chosen by lot rather than by choice.
"Gold tissue" means cloth woven with gold thread; "wonted" means customary.
"Ductile threads" are yarn that can be drawn out in spinning; the nymphs do no ordinary woman's work, only herb-sorting.
"Parched barley" is toasted barley grain, a common ingredient in ancient mixed drinks.
"Quaffed" means drank deeply; "chaunts" elsewhere is an older spelling of chants. Here the drink is Circe's enchanted potion.
"The member with which... I had received the cup" means his hand, now turned into a hoof that leaves footprints.
"The Cyllenian peace-bearer" is Mercury, born on Mount Cyllene, who carries the herald's staff of peace.
"Right hands were exchanged" refers to the clasping of hands as a pledge; Circe's promise is made binding.
"The fissure leaves our cloven feet" means the split hooves close up and become human feet again.
A "chaplet" is a garland or wreath worn on the head, here left as offerings on the statue.

context_notes.text: The beasts are Circe's earlier victims, men turned into animals by her drugs, which explains why they are tame.
Nereids are sea nymphs; here they serve Circe, the sorceress daughter of the Sun, in her palace.
Eurylochus was Ulysses' companion who stayed back from Circe's house, saw what happened, and carried the news to the ship.
Moly is the magical herb from Homer's Odyssey that protects against Circe's drugs; it is called a plant known to the gods.
Macareus is a companion of Ulysses who is telling this story; the statue's tale concerns Picus, turned into a woodpecker by Circe.

literary_notes.text: Fierce beasts behaving gently is unnatural and hints at Circe's magic, preparing the reader for the crew's own transformation.
The beasts' fawning, doglike behavior casts wild animals as courtiers, suggesting they are not truly wild.
Harmful drugs are hidden in a sweet, welcoming drink, which makes the hospitality deceptive.
Macareus breaks off to admit his shame, giving the narrator a human, confessional voice before describing his degradation.
Short clauses mirror the earlier transformation in reverse, so the cure unfolds step by step as the spell's undoing.
The repeated tears and clinging embrace replace speech, showing gratitude too deep for words.
